line: Hi, we're team Processors Assemble: Sarvesh, Aryan, Trishit, Husain and me, Navodit.
We built a RISC-V processor in Verilog, first single-cycle, then a five-stage pipeline, and measured what pipelining really buys on an FPGA.
A five-stage pipeline is ideally five times faster. To test that, we built three CPUs for the same 18-instruction subset.
Single-cycle, a pipeline without forwarding, and one with forwarding. Same tests, same FPGA target.
Every result follows the iron law: time is instructions times CPI over clock.
Single-cycle CPI is one, so a pipeline wins only while its CPI stays below its clock gain: 1.94 without forwarding, 1.43 with it.
The single-cycle datapath runs all 18 instructions in one cycle, so the clock must fit the slowest, a load.
Register read, ALU, memory and write back, in series. That is 17 nanoseconds, 58.75 megahertz.
We cut the same datapath into five stages, with a pipeline register between each pair, and one Verilog module each.
Green lines are the forwarding paths. Red is the branch flush.
Structural hazards cost nothing.
With forwarding, only a load that is used at once stalls, and only for one cycle.
A taken branch flushes two instructions.
Here is how that looks in the Verilog, in the hazard unit.
Line 39. Load use is a load in EX, writing a register that the instruction in ID reads.
Line 43. Flush is just a taken branch in EX.
Line 44. With forwarding, we stall only on load use. Without it, on any result still in EX or MEM.
In the forwarding unit, lines 25 to 28 check EX MEM before MEM WB, so the newest value wins.
Now the demo. make test runs every program on all three CPUs, and checks each one against our Python reference simulator.
248 passed, in under three seconds.
make demo runs the hazard demo on the forwarding pipeline: seven instructions, 14 cycles, one stall, one flush. It also writes a waveform.
At EX PC hex four, forward A and forward B both switch to 2. The add takes x1 straight from EX MEM.
Next, stall goes high for one cycle. The add right after the load waits for its value.
Then flush goes high. The branch is taken in EX, so the two instructions behind it become bubbles.
The same demo as pipeline diagrams from the hardware trace: 14 cycles with forwarding, 19 without.
Without forwarding, a result still in EX or MEM cannot be used yet.
Every program runs on all three CPUs and must match our Python reference simulator: every register, every data word, the instruction count.
248 automated checks, all passing.
Post-route on a Lattice ECP5, pipelining raises the clock from 58.75 to 113.86 megahertz.
Forwarding brings it back to 83.89, because its compare and mux sit in front of the branch decision.
Without forwarding, data stalls dominate. Forwarding removes them.
What is left is load-use stalls and the branch penalty, which adds a quarter to a third of a cycle per instruction in every benchmark.
So the speedup is only 0.71 to 1.29 times, not five.
The critical path is still half to two-thirds of the single-cycle path, and every loop iteration pays two cycles for its branch.
A pipeline wins only when the clock it gains beats the CPI it loses.
Phase II attacks the two losses we measured, branches and the long critical path, then extends the instruction set and runs on a real board. Thank you.
